It is normal for ISPs to set DHCP to offer their own DNS server on each lease. This is by design, and not an issue. If it is not one you want to use, you can manually set your DNS to use a different server such as google's DNS (8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4) or another service like openDNS. From your description of things however, it sounds like DNS is the wrong thing to look at, in regards to being blocked from posting on sites.

As to what they told you,

  1. routers - many people do not set up their home networks properly. Not saying yours was bad, but many people do not understand how to check for sources of interference. I've seen people that are on fiber (50Mbps in this case) only get a few Mbps to their wireless devices because of this. Sometimes really low, like 1Mbps in the worst cases.

  2. Too many devices - If you are on a 2/0.5 Mbps connection, I would say that it is fine to have multiple devices, but performance would suffer to the point that I personally would not want to do that. (assuming all were being used at the same time)

3&4. Trees and weather - these are real things that do affect how radio waves propagate and are absorbed. Can't change how physics work.

  1. bypassing the router - not much to say on this one. It will basically show you what speed they are getting to your location before it goes through other devices that may be impacting the connection. ( Used to determine if #1 is an issue)
  2. worn tab on ethernet cable - This is funny. They just want to see you buy one of theirs. Of course, if the connection is loose, it could cause problems, but I still can't believe how much people will charge for a cheap ass cable. ( I have the same issue with HDMI cables)
  3. Over-subscription - This is normal for ISPs to sell more bandwidth than they have, with the expectation that not everyone will be using it at the same time. I don't feel this is ok anymore. Maybe back in the 90s when websites were smaller and people weren't streaming stuff constantly. Unfortunately, I doubt this practice will change soon.

8,9,&10 viruses and stuff - botnets and such are real, and most common users probably would not notice one that did not delete files or be obnoxious. that being said, the technician at your ISP is probably not qualified to make that call. But, it's at least worth checking out.

Notes on the other stuff: 100% signal is not a thing. Signal strength is usually measured in dB.

WISPs (Wireless Internet Service Providers) are generally a shit way to get internet. It is inherently prone to jitter, causing problems with most real time applications like VoIP or VTC. Also, the frequency range that is available without license is the same your router at home uses. What this ultimately means is that anyone can go buy the equipment and broadcast on those frequencies, effectively jamming your connection, and there is little your ISP can do about it. Spectrum management is very important for WISPs, and I would guess that most of them could do a better job of it.
